Zhaobin Wang*
Abstract: Transition metal-catalyzed radical-based enan-

starting materials. However, existing methods primarily
address precursors with central chirality, neglecting

enantioconvergent reductive coupling of racemic allenes

respectively. Supported by mechanistic insights from
control experiments, deuterium labeling, and DFT
calculations, our approach offers synthetic chemists a
valuable tool for creating enantioenriched chiral homo-

strategies for synthesizing complex chiral molecules.

Introduction
Enantioselective catalysis has significantly transformed or-
ganic synthesis, serving as a practical platform for efficiently
creating chiral molecules in the fields of organic chemistry,
pharmaceuticals, and materials science.<sup>[1]</sup> Notably, the
emergence of transition metal-catalyzed radical-based enan-
tioconvergent reactions stands out as a powerful strategy for
synthesizing enantioenriched molecules.<sup>[2]</sup> This approach
leverages the ready availability and diversity of racemic
starting materials, coupled with the versatile reactivity of
alkyl radicals (Figure 1a). Pioneering studies on Ni-catalytic
radical-based enantioconvergent cross-coupling reactions by
the Fu group<sup>[3]</sup> have not only validated the efficacy of this
methodology but also stimulated the development of more
sophisticated catalytic systems involving first-row transition
metals (Fe, Co, Ni, Cu).<sup>[4]</sup> However, current investigations
have predominantly focused on the radical stereoablation of
racemic precursors bearing central chirality. In stark con-
trast, synthetic methodologies for achieving enantiopure
compounds in a radical-based enantioconvergence manner,
specifically through the stereoablation of other chiral
elements, such as axial chirality, remain elusive.<sup>[5]</sup> The
primary challenge lies in the absence of suitable radical
catalytic systems and reaction models, despite the well-
established protocols for the enantioselective transformation
of racemic allenes or biaryls through dynamic kinetic
asymmetric transformations (DyKATs).<sup>[6]</sup> Notably, recent
exceptional reports describe several examples of site-
selective C(sp<sup>2</sup>)�H cyanation of racemic allenes in moderate
to good enantioselectivity via copper-catalyzed radical
relay.<sup>[7]</sup> Given the importance of radical-based transition-
metal catalysis, there is a persistent need to exploit efficient
catalyst systems to expand the substrate scopes and reaction
patterns.

Allenes, characterized by two cumulative π-bonds dis-
playing axial chirality, represent highly valuable synthetic
precursors in organic chemistry due to their easily accessible
and distinctive chemical properties.<sup>[8]</sup> In particular, stereo-
selective couplings of allenes with carbonyl compounds have
evolved into a versatile platform for accessing diverse chiral
allylic or homoallylic alcohols.<sup>[9]</sup> Diverging from conven-
tional carbonyl additions, these strategies utilize easily
accessible allenes as latent carbanion equivalents, allowing
for better functional group compatibility. In elegant work
using Ir and Ru-based metal-H catalysis, the Krische group
pioneered versatile asymmetric couplings of allenes and
carbonyls under hydrogenation and transfer hydrogenation
conditions.<sup>[10]</sup> However, existing methods have predomi-
nantly focused on the transformations of terminal allenes.<sup>[11]</sup>
In contrast, catalytic enantioconvergent reductive couplings
of racemic allenes and carbonyls, yielding chiral products
with more versatile structural complexity, remain challeng-
ing due to the added difficulty in enhancing the efficiency of
transformation with sterically hindered allenes and control-
ling regio-, and stereoselectivities.<sup>[12]</sup> Additionally, it is
difficult to achieve the stereoablation via a classical
oxidative carbometallation approach which generally pro-
ceed in a stereospecific fashion.<sup>[13]</sup> In this context, excep-
tional works have achieved the asymmetric [3+2] annula-
tion of racemic allenes and imines using chiral phosphine
catalysis<sup>[14]</sup> or Rh catalysis<sup>[15]</sup> in a two-electron nucleophilic
catalysis manner. Nevertheless, a mechanistically distinct
and broadly applicable catalyst system for enantioconver-
gent couplings of these racemic feedstocks remains elusive.
Our recent focus involves the development of radical-
based asymmetric additions to carbonyls, providing access to
enantioenriched alcohols bearing vicinal stereocenters.<sup>[16]</sup> In
this context, we envisioned the stereoablative axial chirality

Results and Discussion
Given the synthetic versatility of sulfonyl groups and the
prevalence of the vinyl sulfone moiety in biological
molecules,<sup>[19]</sup> we initially employed the reductive coupling of
benzaldehyde and allenyl sulfones<sup>[20]</sup> (Table 1). Considering
that the steric and electronic properties of sulfonyl groups
would affect the Zimmerman–Traxler transition states,
different substituted allenyl sulfones were screened (see
Figures S1–S6). To our delight, we found that the E/Z-,
diastereo-, and enantioselectivity (14 :1 E/Z, 15: 1 dr, and
91 % ee) could be well-controlled simultaneously with the
combination of the steric 2,4,6-trimethylbenzenesulfonyl-
substituted allene 2a and the chiral bisoxazoline (R,S)-L1,
affording homoallylic alcohol 3a bearing a vinyl sulfone
moiety in 80 % yield as a single regioisomer (entry 1,
Table 1). The observation of 3a in 80 % yield and 91 % ee
using 1.1 equivalents of 2a strongly suggests an enantiocon-
vergent process rather than kinetic resolution. Control
experiments revealed that CrCl , CoTPP, Ir(dF(CF )ppy) -
(dtbpy)]PF , and light were all essential for this reductive
coupling (entry 2, Table 1). NiCl was ineffective for this
transformation, while TiCl could catalyze the reaction, but
it afforded 3a in poor yield and stereoselectivities (en-
tries 3–4, Table 1). Regarding the chiral ligand, other
bisoxazoline ligands were not suitable under the optimal
condition, providing the desired product 3a with diminished
efficiency (entries 5–8, Table 1). Only a trace amount of the
product was observed when using the chiral diamine ligand
L6 (entry 9, Table 1). Replacing 2a with less sterically
hindered 2b or 2 c led to diminished E/Z ratio and
enantioselectivities (entries 10–11, Table 1), explained by
invoking a Zimmerman–Traxler transition state, wherein the
more sterically hindered sulfonyl group prefers to occupy
the less hindered equatorial position. The use of more
electron-deficient 2d also resulted in decreased stereo
selectivity compared to 2a (entry 12, Table 1). These results
indicate that the steric properties of the allene play a more
important role than electronic properties in controlling
stereoselectivities. Using EtOAc or THF as the solvent
slightly decreased efficiency (entries 13–14, Table 1). The
yield and E/Z ratio significantly diminished when CH CN
was employed as the solvent (entry 15, Table 1).

substrate scope (Scheme 1). To our delight, good to
excellent yields and stereoselectivities were obtained using
various aromatic aldehydes with different substituents on
the para, ortho and meta positions, including trifluorometh-
oxy, boronate, halide, ether, and ester (3 a–3 i). 1-Naphthal-
dehyde also served as a competent substrate (3 j). Various
heteroaromatic aldehydes, including furan, indole, and
pyrimidine proved suitable, yielding satisfactory results (3 k–
3m). Additionally, drug-related aldehyde was smoothly
transformed into the corresponding product with excellent
yield and stereoselectivities (3 n). Unfortunately, alkyl-

to product 3ab with decreased E/Z ratio and enantioselec-

a substrate (3 ac–3ad). Chiral aldehydes, derived from
amino acids, all performed well under optimal conditions,
affording desired products with moderate to good yields,
high E/Z ratios, and excellent diastereoselectivities (3 ae–
3an). Moreover, cholanal was also suitable for this reaction
(3 ao–3ap). It is noteworthy that the stereochemistry of the
chiral catalyst, rather than existing stereocenters on the
aldehydes, predominantly determines the stereochemistry of
the newly formed vicinal stereocenters in coupling products.
We next explored the scope of allenyl sulfones (Scheme 1).
Pleasingly, excellent yields and stereoselectivities were
obtained for a broad array of allenyl sulfones bearing a
primary alkyl substituent (3 aq–3 av). Interestingly, the
terminal alkene was inert under optimal conditions (3at). In
addition, allenyl sulfones bearing a secondary alkyl substitu-
ent, including cyclopropyl, cyclohexyl, and isopropyl, all
reacted effectively with aliphatic aldehyde, furnishing de-
sired homoallylic alcohols in good yields, high E/Z ratios,
and excellent diastereoselectivities (3 aw–3ay). When using
the allenyl sulfone attached to a sterically hindered tert-butyl
group, the reductive coupling proceeded smoothly without
erosion of efficiency, albeit with a slightly diminished yield
(3 az). Notably, the use of 3,3-disubstituted allenyl sulfones
could also afford the desired products in moderate yields
and excellent enantioselectivities (3 ba–3bc). The structure
and absolute configuration of 3as were established by x-ray
crystallographic analysis, and all other compounds with an E
configuration vinyl sulfone moiety were assigned by analogy
accordingly.
Z-alkenes widely exist as basic structural motifs in
natural products and bioactive compounds. However, com-
pared to the preparation of E-alkenes, their efficient and
highly selective synthesis remains a challenge.<sup>[21]</sup> In this
context, we further optimized the reaction conditions for
generating products with Z configured carbon-carbon
double bond. After carefully investigating various reaction
parameters (see Figures S7–S9), we determined optimal
conditions with 4-methylbenzenesulfonyl as the protecting
group, bisoxazoline (S,R)-L4 as the chiral ligand, and
EtOAc as the solvent. Critically, the use of MgCl as an
additive was crucial to improving enantioselectivity. Then,
we investigated the substrate scopes for Z-alkene selectivity
(Scheme 2). The enantioconvergent reductive coupling re-
action proceeded effectively to afford the desired products
in good yields with moderate Z/E ratios when using a variety
of aromatic aldehydes bearing substituents on the para,
ortho or meta position. Nevertheless, excellent stereoselec-
tivities for Z-alkene were achieved (4 a–4 g). Heterocyclic
aldehyde furfural was also a competent substrate (4 h). In
contrast, the use of aliphatic aldehyde led to slightly
decreased stereoselectivities (4 i, 7 : 1 dr, 80 % ee). Regarding
the scope of allenyl sulfones, the alkyl substituent on allenes
could range in steric demand from methyl, n-pentyl,
cyclohexyl to tert-butyl, providing desired products in
moderate to good yields and excellent stereoselectivities
were still obtained for Z-alkenes (4j–4l). Despite the
moderate control of Z/E ratio under these cases, this
protocol offers a new access to chiral homoallylic alcohols
bearing a Z/E defined alkene unit in a mechanistically
distinct radical enantioconvergent manner.

generating products with Z configured carbon-carbon

additive was crucial to improving enantioselectivity. Then,

Allenyl esters are versatile synthons in organic synthesis,

Conclusion
In conclusion, we have developed a radical-based enantio-
convergent reductive coupling of racemic allenes and
aldehydes via photoredox/Cr/Co triple catalysis. This meth-
od furnishes a broad range of synthetically versatile chiral
homoallylic alcohols bearing an internal carbon-carbon
double bond with excellent efficiency, selectivity, and func-
tional group tolerance. The robustness of the protocol is
highlighted by its broad substrate scope, including various
aromatic, heteroaromatic, aliphatic aldehydes and chiral
aldehydes. The reductive coupling products could be readily
transformed into a series of valuable chiral building blocks,
demonstrating the potential synthetic utility of this protocol.
Preliminary mechanistic studies, including TEMPO inhib-
ition, control experiments and time-course study, unambigu-
ously suggest that this protocol proceeds in a radical-based
enantioconvergence manner. Deuterium-labeling experi-
ments and DFT calculations provide insights into the origin
of regio- and stereoselectivity. We anticipate that this
protocol will become a valuable tool for synthetic chemists,
offering efficient access to enantioenriched chiral homoal-
lylic alcohols with a stereo-defined internal carbon-carbon
double bond.
